paras: The Kevil depot fight and expulsion of Black residents was a clash between Black men and white youths at Kevil, an Illinois Central station in Ballard County, Kentucky, on October 11, 1903, followed by the flight of the area's Black residents from armed white neighbors. A white youth, Crockett Childress, was mortally wounded, and a Black man, Tom Hall, was shot in the arm, arrested, and on October 16 lynched at Wickliffe. White papers called it a "race riot," while the St. Paul Appeal blamed the separation of the platform by color.
Kevil was a small station a few miles west of Paducah where, according to the Paducah Sun, one platform was "set apart for the colored people."

According to the Sun, about 6:30 p.m. three white youths, Tom Scott, Bernard Reed and Childress, walked past the Black platform and were told, "according to reports," to "pass on by and not stop." After words were exchanged, the Sun said, the Black men advanced with knives, razors and pistols, Hall dueled with Reed, and a bullet that missed Reed struck Childress near the heart. Reed's shot hit Hall in the arm. The Owingsville Outlook said instead that about 25 Black railroad hands had driven whites, including women, off the platform, and that a Black man fired six shots at the returning youths.

Officers detained Hall at Maxon Mills and brought him to Paducah. The next day, according to the Sun, men from the area bought guns in Paducah until "every man in the locality of the imbroglio was a walking arsenal before night," and the Black residents, hearing of it, left in twos and threes. An Associated Press dispatch said the whites had been "preparing to run the negroes out," and the Outlook reported an attempt to organize a mob "to run down the blacks and kill them." The Sun predicted Kevil would become "a second Calvert City, where colored people are not allowed to stop over night."

On October 15 Sheriff Lee Potter took Hall to the Wickliffe jail; Hall said another man had fired the shot. Early the next day a mob of about one hundred took him from the jail and hanged him to a tree in the jail yard, after he had named Jim Rivers as the shooter. Black residents were reported still leaving Kevil, "badly frightened" by the lynching.

Childress, a nephew of Paducah Coroner William Peal, died on October 20; the Sun then wrote that "it is claimed" Hall shot him and that he was lynched by "men supposed to be friends of young Childress." Hall's mother wrote from Mississippi that she had no money to come and had not known he was lynched. No report of an inquest or of any other arrest was found, and on November 2 a false lynching report at Kevil caused "much uneasiness."

White coverage began with a Paducah wire, "Race Riot in Kentucky" in the Washington Evening Star, which called Hall "a negro desperado" and ran in Indianapolis, Bismarck, Bemidji and Huntington. The local Sun praised the youths who "bravely stood their ground" and spoke of a "miniature race war," while the Outlook's headline read "A Negro in Cold Blood Killed a White Boy." Later headlines included "Kentucky Whites Run Negroes Out Country" in the St. Paul Globe and, for the lynching, "Kentucky Mob Hangs White Lad's Slayer" in Santa Fe.

The only Black-press item found, an October 17 St. Paul Appeal editorial, blamed "the color line separations which are in vogue in the South." Reversing the white account, it said white "children" had gone onto the Black portion of the platform, and that Black residents "have had to flee for their lives"; it did not mention Hall.

White papers said Black men ordered whites off their platform; the Appeal said whites entered the Black portion. The shooter of Childress was variously Hall, an unnamed Black man, or, in Hall's account, Jim Rivers, and the Sun's last report said only "some negro in a crowd."

reader.title: Kevil depot fight and expulsion of Black residents
bases: After the October 11 platform shooting, white residents armed themselves to 'run the negroes out' and the Black residents of the Kevil section fled (A3, A7, A23); the clash itself was a mutual fight (A2, A12), and the lynching of Tom Hall at Wickliffe on October 16 (A14) is the table's separate event g144.

The local Paducah Sun (A2, A3), the Associated Press wires (A1, A7, A14) and the Owingsville Outlook (A12) independently report the fight, the shootings of Childress and Hall and the flight of Black residents, and the St. Paul Appeal (A23) confirms the flight, though they disagree on who began the fight and who shot Childress.

framing.detail: Wire headlines 'Race Riot in Kentucky' and 'Negroes Ordered Whites Off Station Platform and Shooting Began' put the cause on Black people; Hall called a 'negro desperado'.

The Paducah Sun praised the white youths who 'bravely stood their ground,' called Hall 'ringleader' and 'desperado,' but attributed the Black men's words to 'reports' and by Oct 21 wrote only that 'it is claimed' Hall shot Childress.
The Owingsville Outlook headed its story 'A Negro in Cold Blood Killed a White Boy'; lynching wires ran as 'Kentucky Mob Hangs White Lad's Slayer' and 'Mob's Revenge on Negro Who Shot a White Boy'.
Expulsion reported flatly: 'Kentucky Whites Run Negroes Out Country', 'Negroes Flee From Kevil'.
St. Paul Appeal editorial blamed 'color line separations' for the death and the 'threatened race war' and noted Black residents had to flee for their lives.
